blocks.text: And Aelian, History, book 8, chapter 13: Περὶ Κόρκυραν δὲ γίνονται καλέμεναι ὕδραι· αἵπερουν τοὺς διώκοντας (read πρὸς τοὺς διώκοντας) ἐπιστραφεῖσαι, καὶ φυσήσασαι πνεῦμα ἄτομον, εἶτα ἀναστέλλουσι τῆς ὁρμῆς, καὶ ἀποστρέφουσι [Peri Korkyran de ginontai kalemenai hydrai· haiperoun tous diōkontas (pros tous diōkontas) epistrapheisai, kai physēsasai pneuma atomon, eita anastellousi tēs hormēs, kai apostrephousi]. But in Corcyra hydrae are bred which, turning upon their pursuers and breathing out a heavy breath, check their onset and drive them away.

I see one possible objection: that hydri are born and reared in watery places, and it is reasonable to suppose that the desert of the Israelites lacked such places, above all in the part where they were bitten by the serpents, since these serpents were sent against them for the very reason that they had murmured against God and Moses for lack of water, Num. XXI, 5. 6. But this objection can be met in several ways. 1. Even if the Israelites, faint with thirst, lacked drinkable water, it does not at once follow that there were no marshy and muddy waters in the desert in which hydri might lurk. Nicander at any rate states that hydri mostly live ἐπὶ βροχθώδει λίμνῃ [epi brochthōdei limnē], that [III, 216] is, ἀνύδρῳ, ἢ ξηρᾷ, ἢ ὀλίγον ὕδωρ ἐχούσῃ [anydrō, ē xēra, ē oligon hydōr echousē], in a waterless lake, or a dry one, or one having little water, as the Scholiast interprets it. 2. Moreover it is known (and we have already proved it above ^{p)}) that hydri, when water fails, do not at once die but become chersydri, and by this very fact truly seraphim, that is, burning and scorching. It is probable that the same happened here, and that those serpents' bite was then more dangerous, because the heat had consumed the water even from the marshes. That this conjecture is not idle is shown by the season. For Nicander adds that hydri become chersydri and beset the roads around the Dog Days:
— — — — ὅταν ὕδωρ Σείριος ἀζήνῃσι, τρύγη δ' ἐνὶ πυθμένι λίμνης· [— — — — hotan hydōr Seirios azēnēsi, trygē d' eni pythmeni limnēs·]

When the Dog Star has dried up the water, and there is dryness at the bottom of the lake. Now see and weigh, reader, at what season of the year this calamity fell upon the Israelites. Aaron died on Mount Hor on the first day of the fifth month, Num. XXXIII, 38, that is, the month Ab or Abba (so read in Josephus instead of Σαββὰ [Sabba], Antiquities, book 4, chapter 4). The date corresponds to the nineteenth of July. The Israelites mourned him for thirty days, Num. XX, 29. Immediately there was a battle against the king of Arad. Then came the murmuring of the people and the sending of the serpents, Num. XXI. So this must have happened around the end of August, as the sun was leaving the Dog Star. 3. Finally, even granting that that part of the desert lacked water at every season of the year, watery places were nevertheless not far off. For on the first march, Num. XXI, 10, the people came to a place called Oboth (that is, wineskins), probably because there they not only drank but also refilled the skins long empty. The second march was to Ije-abarim, that is, heaps of the fords, or, as the Chaldees explain it, the ford of those crossing. The third to the brook Zered. The fourth to the river Arnon. The fifth to Beer, that is, the well, celebrated in Scripture in splendid words, Num. XXI, 17. 18. Hence we read in Deut. X, 7 that the Israelites, shortly after the death of Aaron, came into a land watered by rivers of water. So let no one imagine that this desert was everywhere dry and waterless. Hydri born in these or similar places, whether creeping or even flying, could therefore be sent by God against the Israelites. This seems to be inferable from the words of Moses, The Lord sent among the people Seraphim serpents. By these words, I say, the divine writer clearly hints that these serpents were not born there, but were summoned from elsewhere by a certain force θεηλάτῳ [theēlatō], to punish the stubborn people. Just as in Egypt the frogs, leaving their natural place, that is, the rivers, streams and marshes, covered the whole land like a cloud, so that they even climbed the upper [III, 217] storeys of the houses. Accordingly it is said of the serpents sent by God, [col. 425] Sap. XVI, 5. Ἐπῆλθε θηρίων θυμός [Epēlthe thēriōn thymos]· The poison of serpents came upon them (as if unexpectedly).
